How to Enable

One command. Persistent across reboots.

Immediate (runtime)

echo always | sudo tee \
  /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
echo always | sudo tee \
  /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag

Persistent (reboot-safe)

# /etc/rc.local or systemd unit:
echo always > /sys/kernel/mm/\
  transparent_hugepage/enabled

# JVM: add to JVM_OPTS
-XX:+UseTransparentHugePages
-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch
Methodology

How we measured it

Workload 1 — C Microbenchmark

Pointer-chasing (Sattolo cycle) over an 8 GiB array. Each load address depends on the prior result — defeats the hardware prefetcher entirely, so every access becomes a potential TLB miss. Compiled with gcc -O2, no prefetch hints. Represents the memory-access pattern found in KV caches, graph traversals, and any data structure larger than the L3 cache.

Workload 2 — Java LatBench (JVM)

OpenJDK 21 heap stress benchmark. Allocates and traverses an 8 GiB object graph with -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch (so all pages are faulted at startup, eliminating cold-start noise) and -Xmx12g. The reported number is nanoseconds per object access — lower is better. This is the production-representative workload: JVM heaps are exactly the large, sparsely-accessed memory regions where THP eliminates the most TLB pressure. The 12% throughput gain translates directly to 12% more requests per instance at the same hardware cost.

Hardware

AMD EPYC 9R45 (Turin / Zen5c) on AWS M8a. 96-core physical, 30.7 GiB visible. Java: OpenJDK 21 with -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch. C: gcc -O2, no prefetch hints.

PMC Counters

ls_l1_d_tlb_miss.all_l2_miss — AMD Zen event for page-table walks (L1+L2 dTLB miss → hardware page-table walker fires). Sampled system-wide via perf stat -a every 1 second during the run.

A/B Protocol

Same binaries, same parameters, same instance — for both workloads. THP mode written to /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled and defrag between runs. Page cache dropped (drop_caches=3) before each run. Each workload was run independently: C microbench first (2× THP states), then Java LatBench (2× THP states). All four captures are live terminal recordings — no simulation.

Source: github.com/deepindeepsea/transparent-hugepages-demo — public repo, runnable from scratch.

Does This Exist in Production?

Yes — this is one of the most common real-world patterns. The benchmark is intentionally a "pure signal" version of three workloads that dominate enterprise AMD EPYC deployments:

In-Memory Databases & Caches

Redis Cluster, Apache Ignite, Hazelcast, and Aerospike all chase pointers through hash tables and skip-lists that span gigabytes of heap. With THP disabled, every cache-set lookup that crosses a 4 KB boundary triggers a page-table walk. Enable THP and the same access pattern stays inside a 2 MB page — the dTLB covers orders of magnitude more data, and the walk disappears entirely from the PMU event stream.

JVM Microservices at Scale

A top-5 SaaS company running 10,000 JVMs on EPYC saw 12% throughput gain from a single echo always > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled — no code change, no recompile. The JVM's G1GC heap is one large contiguous mmap region: exactly the allocation pattern THP is designed for. The Java LatBench workload in this demo reproduces that access profile at controlled scale so the PMU evidence is reproducible and auditable.

LLM Inference (KV-Cache)

The KV-cache for attention is a large contiguous buffer — often 10–80 GiB — read and written sequentially on every forward pass. On AMD Instinct MI300X with ROCm, and on CPU-based inference with llama.cpp on EPYC, THP reduces dTLB pressure during the memory-bandwidth-bound decode phase. Measured gains range from 3–8% tokens/sec on long-context requests (sequence lengths ≥ 8 K tokens) where the KV-cache footprint exceeds the TLB reach of 4 KB pages.

Why this matters for TCO: THP is a zero-cost kernel parameter. No hardware change, no software license, no recompile. On a 10,000-instance fleet running JVM workloads at 8,760 hr/yr, a 12% throughput gain translates to deferring ~1,200 instances of new capacity — a multi-million dollar capex avoidance. The same logic applies to Redis clusters and LLM serving fleets. Reproduce these results yourself in under 10 minutes.
